reply_text:
*I’d hold the merge.* Reviewed `http-retries` (`b04b610`) against `main` (`5f9be03`). Found four issues:

1. *High — `timeoutMs: 0` no longer disables timeouts* — `src/http.js:11`  
   `opts.timeoutMs || DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS` replaces zero with 10,000. This breaks the documented behavior and the existing nightly-export caller. Exports taking more than 10 seconds to return response headers will now abort. Confirmed that `downloadExport()` arms a 10,000ms timer. Preserve zero with `??`, as on `main`.

2. *High — automatic retries can duplicate writes* — `src/http.js:30–33`  
   Retries apply to every HTTP method, including POST, without opt-in or an idempotency guarantee. A server can commit a write and still return 503; retrying then repeats the operation. In a local-server reproduction, one `request()` call produced *two server-side writes* before returning 200. Restrict default retries to safe operations; require explicit authorization/idempotency for writes.

3. *Medium — streamed request bodies cannot be replayed* — `src/http.js:31`  
   Each attempt reuses the same `init.body`. With a real streamed POST returning 503, the second attempt threw `TypeError: Response body object should not be disturbed or locked`. Either exclude non-replayable bodies from retries or accept a fresh-body factory.

4. *Medium — discarded responses aren’t drained or cancelled* — `src/http.js:32–33`  
   Retried responses are abandoned without consuming or cancelling their bodies. With real Fetch responses, this can retain connections/resources and exhaust a bounded connection pool during an outage—the exact time retries become frequent. Release each discarded response before retrying, leaving the final response untouched.

*Validation:* All three existing tests pass, but none covers these cases. I also ran read-only, in-memory reproductions with real Fetch/local HTTP for the duplicate-write and streamed-body failures. No files were changed; the working tree remains clean.
